Sensitivity Analysis for Sample Size Planning From the Accuracy in Parameter Estimation Perspective for the Standardized Regression Coefficient

Source: R/ss_aipe_src_sensitivity.R
ss_aipe_src_sensitivity.Rd

Performs a sensitivity analysis when planning sample size from the Accuracy in Parameter Estimation Perspective for the standardized regression coefficient. ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity and ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity are the counterparts for the unstandardized coefficient.

Usage

ss_aipe_src_sensitivity(
  true_var_Y = NULL,
  true_cov_YX = NULL,
  true_cov_XX = NULL,
  supposed_var_Y = NULL,
  supposed_cov_YX = NULL,
  supposed_cov_XX = NULL,
  specified_N = NULL,
  which_predictor = 1,
  width = NULL,
  noncentral = TRUE,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  assurance = NULL,
  G = 1000,
  print_iter = TRUE,
  filename = NULL,
  assurance_method = c("analytic", "simulation"),
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

true_var_Y

Population variance of the dependent variable (Y)

true_cov_YX

Population covariances vector between the p predictor variables and the dependent variable (Y)

true_cov_XX

Population covariance matrix of the p predictor variables

supposed_var_Y

Supposed variance of the dependent variable (Y), the planning value from which the sample size is planned

supposed_cov_YX

Supposed covariances vector (planning values) between the p predictor variables and the dependent variable (Y)

supposed_cov_XX

Supposed covariance matrix (planning values) of the p predictor variables

specified_N

Directly specified sample size (instead of planning one from the supposed covariance structure)

which_predictor

identifies which of the p predictors is of interest

width

Desired confidence interval width for the standardized regression coefficient of interest

noncentral

TRUE (the default) for the noncentral t interval for the standardized coefficient (that of ci_src), FALSE for the central t interval of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 1). The interval of each replication is that interval, and a sample size planned from the supposed values is planned for it by ss_aipe_src with the same noncentral.

conf_level

desired level of confidence for the computed interval (i.e., 1 - the Type I error rate)

assurance

degree of certainty that the obtained confidence interval will be sufficiently narrow

G

the number of generations/replication of the simulation study within the function

print_iter

specify with a TRUE/FALSE statement if the iteration number should be printed as the simulation within the function runs

filename

Optional path of a CSV file to receive the per-replication results (the standardized coefficient estimate std_reg_coef_j, its confidence limits ci_lower and ci_upper, the observed \(R^2\) R2, the standard error se_std_reg_coef_j, and the t statistic t_value), appended when the file already exists and created otherwise; the default NULL writes nothing, and a throwaway run that wants the file should point it at tempfile(fileext = ".csv").

assurance_method

Passed to ss_aipe_src, which plans the sample size from the supposed values with assurance: "analytic" (the default) for the published approximation, which does not compute the probability of an interval no wider than width (for the noncentral interval that of MBESS, and for the central one the chi square approximation of Kelley and Maxwell, 2003, Equation 3), at unit standard deviations; "simulation" for the smallest sample size at which a simulated estimate of that probability, made by the planner from its default G of 20000 samples with the random number stream that seed sets, is at least assurance. Not used with specified_N or without assurance.

seed

NULL (the default) to draw from the current random number stream, or a single number that makes the call reproducible; a supplied seed is set for this call only, and the caller's random number state is restored when the function returns.

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value summarizing the Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis: mean / median / SD summaries of the realized standardized regression coefficient (mean_std_reg_coef_j, median_std_reg_coef_j, sd_std_reg_coef_j), the realized interval widths (mean_ci_width, median_ci_width, sd_ci_width), and the realized squared multiple correlation coefficient (mean_R2, median_R2, sd_R2); the proportion of intervals at or below the planning target (pct_ci_less_width); the tail-specific and overall empirical non-coverage of the population standardized coefficient (pct_ci_miss_low, pct_ci_miss_high, total_type_I_error), all proportions on the 0 to 1 scale; and the input echoes (total_N, p, which_predictor, true_std_reg_coef_j and supposed_std_reg_coef_j, the population and planning values of the standardized coefficient implied by the covariance structures, width, conf_level, and, when one was supplied, assurance). The per-replication file written with filename has the columns std_reg_coef_j, ci_lower, ci_upper, R2, se_std_reg_coef_j, and t_value.

Details

Direct specification of true_cov_YX and true_cov_XX is necessary, even if one is interested in a single regression coefficient, so that the covariance/correlation structure can be specified when the simulation study within the function runs.

The coefficient. The data of every replication are standardized with their own sample standard deviations before the regression is fit, so each estimate and each interval is for the standardized coefficient, the quantity true_std_reg_coef_j of ss_aipe_src stands for. The true value the intervals are judged against is the population standardized coefficient $$\beta_j = b_j \sigma_{X_j} / \sigma_Y,$$ the unstandardized coefficient \(b_j\) (the jth element of \(\Sigma_{XX}^{-1}\sigma_{XY}\), from true_cov_XX and true_cov_YX) multiplied by the ratio of the population standard deviations (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003, p. 316), where \(\sigma_Y\) is the square root of true_var_Y and \(\sigma_{X_j}\) the square root of the jth diagonal element of true_cov_XX. The supposed coefficient is put on the same scale with the supposed standard deviations (supposed_var_Y and the diagonal of supposed_cov_XX), and a sample size planned from the supposed values is planned by ss_aipe_src for a coefficient on that scale, with the supposed correlations and the same noncentral, so that width is a width in the units of the intervals simulated and the plan is for the interval simulated.

The plan with assurance. With noncentral = FALSE and assurance, the plan is that of ss_aipe_src for the central interval for the standardized coefficient: by default the chi square approximation of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 3), and with assurance_method = "simulation" the smallest sample size at which that interval is no wider than width with at least that probability. For two predictors correlated .3 with correlations of .4 and .3 with Y, a width of .3, and an assurance of .90, the approximation is 181, at which .986 of the standardized intervals are no wider than .3, and the simulated plan is 171 (another seed can give one a case away; see ss_aipe_src).

The interval of each replication is that of ci_reg_coef with the standard error of the regression fitted to the standardized data. That standard error treats the sample standard deviations as constants, so it is approximate, and the predictors simulated here are random, so those of the predictors vary along with that of Y (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003, pp. 315–316; see ci_src); the coverage rows show how good the approximation is for the structure given.

Note

Note that when the true and supposed covariance structures agree (true_cov_YX equals supposed_cov_YX and true_cov_XX equals supposed_cov_XX), the results are not literally from a sensitivity analysis, rather the function performs a standard simulation study. A simulation study can be helpful in order to determine if the sample size procedure under or overestimates necessary sample size. See ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity in DMAR for more details.

The record of the simulation

Every sensitivity function of the package summarizes its replications over one denominator: the replications that produced a confidence interval (for a power sensitivity function, a test). The proportion of intervals that met the width target (pct_ci_less_width), the proportions of intervals that missed the true value, and the summaries of the widths are all taken over those replications. A replication without an interval is in none of these rows. It is counted, and the returned table carries the counts in its attribute simulation, a list read with attr(x, "simulation"):

attempted

the number of replications asked for (G).

returned

the number that produced an interval (a test).

failed

the number that did not (attempted - returned).

denominator

the number of replications the rows named above are taken over, which is returned.

width_target_probability

the proportion of the replications with an interval whose interval met the width target, the value of the pct_ci_less_width row; NA for a function or a call without a width target, and when no replication produced an interval.

width_target_mc_ci

the exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) limits for that proportion, at the confidence level of the table. They describe the error of the simulation, which shrinks as G grows, and nothing else.

A function that records more about its run adds elements to the list, and its help page names them. The line "Replications" beneath the printed table gives G, and the three counts when a replication was without an interval. With many replications without an interval the rows describe only the studies in which the interval could be formed, so failed is to be reported beside them.

References

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 4 on individual comparisons of means and Chapter 6 on trend analysis.)

See also

ss_aipe_src, ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity, ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity, ss_aipe_reg_coef, ci_reg_coef

Examples

# Sensitivity analysis for a standardized regression coefficient
# with two correlated predictors. A production run uses many more
# generations (G = 1000 is typical); G is reduced here so the
# example runs quickly.
set.seed(113)
cov_XX  <- matrix(c(1, 0.3, 0.3, 1), nrow = 2)
cov_YX  <- c(0.4, 0.3)
ss_aipe_src_sensitivity(
  true_var_Y = 1, true_cov_YX = cov_YX, true_cov_XX = cov_XX,
  supposed_var_Y = 1, supposed_cov_YX = cov_YX, supposed_cov_XX = cov_XX,
  which_predictor = 1, width = 0.20, conf_level = 0.95,
  G = 50, print_iter = FALSE
)
#>  term                    value
#>  mean_std_reg_coef_j     0.339
#>  median_std_reg_coef_j   0.342
#>  sd_std_reg_coef_j       0.045
#>  mean_ci_width           0.200
#>  median_ci_width         0.200
#>  sd_ci_width             0.004
#>  pct_ci_less_width       0.560
#>  pct_ci_miss_low         0.000
#>  pct_ci_miss_high        0.020
#>  total_type_I_error      0.020
#>  mean_R2                 0.197
#>  median_R2               0.198
#>  sd_R2                   0.033
#>  total_N                 365  
#>  p                       2    
#>  which_predictor         1    
#>  true_std_reg_coef_j     0.341
#>  supposed_std_reg_coef_j 0.341
